paragraphs: Examples placed in a language model’s prompt can help it answer a new question, but their usefulness depends on both relevance and order. AutoSelect treats choosing these demonstrations as a sequence of decisions. Each choice considers the query together with the examples already selected, allowing the framework to account for their combined context.

The method represents that context using matrices intended to preserve structural information, then trains a policy to choose the next example. Its optimization includes a KL regularization term and connects the optimal policy to a Plackett-Luce ranking of demonstration sequences. The authors prove that a tractable cross-entropy training loss bounds the worst-case discrepancy between the learned ranking and the optimal ranking.

This connection matters because the number of possible example orderings grows factorially, making exhaustive comparison impractical. Across nine datasets, AutoSelect beats heuristic and learned selection methods, with improvements reaching 11% over the strongest baseline. Additional analyses support its transferability and generalizability, while the theoretical result explains how a manageable training objective can guide selection among many possible sequences.
icml-2026-auto-regressive-in-context-dem.tldr: AutoSelect learns to choose prompt examples sequentially, accounting for their context and order while improving performance across nine datasets.

paragraphs: An embodied model can fail a task because it misperceives a scene, misunderstands movement, or plans poorly. A single task score does little to separate these causes. BEAR evaluates smaller component skills, providing a more detailed picture of where multimodal language models struggle when interpreting and acting in physical environments.

The benchmark contains 4,469 entries combining images, video, and text. It covers 14 atomic skills grouped into six categories, extending from perception to planning. A hierarchical diagnosis of 20 models identifies perception as a major bottleneck behind reasoning failures. It also reveals unstable modeling of space and time that earlier benchmarks had left unexposed.

The authors use these findings to build BEAR-Agent, which equips multimodal models with visual and spatial tools. It improves performance across skills, including a 17.5% relative gain for GPT-5 on BEAR, and substantially outperforms baselines in simulation and real-robot experiments across models. The contribution therefore connects finer evaluation to a concrete intervention: identifying weak capabilities helps motivate tools that address those weaknesses.
icml-2026-bear-dissecting-embodied-abili.tldr: BEAR diagnoses embodied models at the skill level and uses the findings to motivate tool assistance that improves benchmark and robot performance.

paragraphs: Music models need a representation that turns notes and timing into tokens. Common approaches encode events such as pitches, note starts, and time shifts. These representations work well with Transformers, but advancing by one token does not correspond to advancing by a fixed amount of musical time. Regular timing is therefore represented only indirectly.

BEAT organizes symbolic music around equal-length time steps, such as beats. Within each step, it combines all events at the same pitch into a token, then explicitly groups tokens by that step. The resulting representation resembles a sparse piano roll: pitch and time remain central, while tokens describe the events occurring at particular positions.

The authors compare this tokenization with mainstream event-based alternatives on music continuation and accompaniment generation. They report better musical quality and structural coherence, alongside analyses showing greater efficiency and stronger capture of long-range patterns. These findings suggest that making regular musical time explicit can help models organize generated music beyond individual note events, connecting the choice of input representation to both computational behavior and musical structure.
icml-2026-beat-tokenizing-and-generating.tldr: BEAT groups symbolic music into uniform time steps, improving generation quality, structural coherence, and efficiency in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Finding an answer inside an instructional video requires locating the particular moment that addresses a question. This is difficult when a long recording contains only a short relevant segment, especially if the question demands more than recognizing an object or action. Irrelevant footage can distract retrieval methods, while weak visual reasoning can prevent accurate selection.

CACR separates the task into candidate generation and reasoning. A selection algorithm based on visual-language pre-training first produces K possible answer segments. A temporal logic reasoning module then operates on those candidates. Its training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization and a rejection reward mechanism, combining a narrowed search space with an explicitly trained reasoning stage.

Across six benchmarks, the method achieves state-of-the-art mean Intersection-over-Union, which measures how well predicted segments overlap the target moments. The result supports the value of selecting plausible regions before reasoning about their suitability. For direct video answer retrieval, better overlap means that the returned interval more closely matches the part of the recording needed to answer the query.
icml-2026-cacr-reinforcing-temporal-answ.tldr: CACR combines candidate video segments with reinforcement-trained temporal reasoning to locate answer moments more accurately.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can generate statements unsupported by its image or text inputs. Increasing attention to image tokens might seem helpful, but some image regions already attract attention despite being irrelevant. Simply amplifying existing attention can strengthen this problem. It can also leave the model paying too little attention to what the user actually asked.

GIFT instead tracks increases in visual attention while the model processes the query. These changes, described as gaze shifts, produce a visual saliency map before answer generation. During each decoding step, the method strengthens attention to both salient image information and the user query. The approach relies on the observation that irrelevant attention sinks show relatively little change during query comprehension.

Experiments cover both generative and classification tasks and report hallucination mitigation, with gains reaching 20.7% over greedy decoding. General vision-language performance is maintained with low computational overhead. The findings support using query-related changes in attention to guide visual emphasis, while treating attention to the question itself as part of the same fusion problem.
icml-2026-capturing-gaze-shifts-for-guid.tldr: GIFT uses query-driven shifts in visual attention to strengthen relevant image and text signals, reducing hallucinations with low overhead.

paragraphs: Watermarks can help identify whether a text-to-image diffusion model belongs to a particular owner. Existing backdoor-based approaches often assume that querying a suspicious model will faithfully reveal its watermark behavior. The paper challenges that assumption: intentional attacks or other changes can damage the signal and make ownership verification less reliable.

Cert-LAS combines watermark embedding with layer-adaptive smoothing. It uses diffusion classifiers and an LFS-guided noise mechanism that varies across layers. Verification then becomes a statistical comparison: a hypothesis test checks whether the suspicious model responds more strongly to the watermark than unwatermarked reference models do. This gives the ownership decision an explicit reference-based testing procedure.

The authors prove that reliable verification remains possible under certain conditions even when an adversary attempts watermark removal. The certification is therefore conditional, rather than a guarantee against every modification. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness and resistance to adaptive attacks. Together, the theory and evaluation address the gap between embedding a recognizable watermark and retaining enough evidence to verify ownership after the model has been altered.
icml-2026-cert-las-toward-certified-mode.tldr: Cert-LAS combines layer-adaptive smoothing and statistical testing to support diffusion-model ownership verification, with conditional guarantees against watermark removal.

paragraphs: Being good at an individual task does not ensure that a language-model agent will cooperate effectively with a partner. Collaboration requires communication to influence actions in a shared situation, while accommodating different partner behaviors. CollabBench studies these demands through cooperative games, where conversational choices are tied to behavior and task execution.

The framework includes a simulation pipeline for generating diverse player profiles and a training approach that combines reasoning, communication, and action within agent interaction sequences. Its reward balances task efficiency with affective adaptation, so successful cooperation is assessed along both dimensions. The authors also extend game environments into CWAH-MultiPlayer and Cook-MultiPlayer to evaluate collaboration across varied personalities.

The trained models outperform their base versions, with reported gains of 19.5% in efficiency and 24.4% in affective performance. Further analysis identifies limitations in existing models’ collaborative behavior. These results show improvements within the benchmark’s cooperative settings and demonstrate why measuring task completion alongside adaptation to partners offers a fuller account of collaboration than conversation-only evaluation.
icml-2026-collabbench-benchmarking-and-u.tldr: CollabBench evaluates and trains cooperation with diverse simulated partners, improving both task efficiency and affective performance.

paragraphs: Federated class-incremental learning asks distributed models to recognize new classes while retaining earlier knowledge. Replaying selected examples from older classes can help, but choosing representative examples is difficult when data are distributed. Local selection may miss the broader distribution, while approaches that build global feature spaces face a tension between effectiveness and privacy.

CLIF selects replay examples by combining importance estimates from several feature perspectives. Its first module computes Lewis weights for each view and fuses them into a more consistent assessment of sample importance. The aim is to make the retained subset better reflect the global data distribution. A second module weights training losses according to how frequently each sample is selected across views.

The two modules connect example selection with the influence those examples receive during learning: samples repeatedly identified as important receive greater emphasis. The paper provides theoretical analysis supporting the method and reports consistent baseline improvements of 1%–6% across three datasets. These findings support using multiple perspectives to improve replay quality in distributed continual learning, without establishing a separate quantified privacy guarantee in the abstract.
icml-2026-cross-view-lewis-weight-fusion.tldr: CLIF combines sample-importance estimates across feature views to improve replay selection and training in federated class-incremental learning.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel and need not follow a fixed left-to-right order. Turning that flexibility into useful speed is difficult because decoding more tokens together can reduce accuracy. d3LLM addresses this tradeoff through changes to both model training and the procedure used to generate text.

During training, pseudo-trajectory distillation teaches the model which tokens can be predicted confidently in early decoding steps. At inference time, entropy-based multi-block decoding works with a mechanism for refreshing the key-value cache. These components are designed to increase parallel generation while preserving accuracy. The paper also introduces Accuracy Under Parallelism, a metric that evaluates the two objectives together.

Reported experiments achieve speedups of up to ten times over vanilla LLaDA and Dream, and up to five times over autoregressive models, without much accuracy loss. These are maximum reported gains rather than uniform improvements across every setting. The contribution is a coordinated training and inference strategy that makes parallel decoding more useful, alongside an evaluation measure that keeps accuracy visible when comparing generation speed.
icml-2026-d3llm-ultra-fast-diffusion-llm.tldr: d3LLM combines confidence-focused distillation and parallel decoding to accelerate diffusion language models without much accuracy loss.

paragraphs: When a language model answers using supplied context, its attention patterns provide clues about how it uses that material. Earlier detectors summarize those patterns coarsely, which can hide rapid changes. This paper asks whether the variation within attention carries useful evidence of contextual hallucination, rather than looking only at broad measures of attention allocation.

The authors treat attention distributions as discrete signals and extract their high-frequency components. Here, high frequency refers to rapid local changes in attention. Their analysis associates hallucinated tokens with higher energy in these components, interpreting the pattern as fragmented and unstable grounding. They then turn those features into a lightweight detector that uses signals available during generation.

On RAGTruth and HalluRAG, the detector improves over methods based on verification, internal representations, and other attention features across the tested models and tasks. The finding supports attention instability as a useful detection signal. It establishes an association that helps classification, rather than claiming that every rapid attention change proves a hallucination or that attention alone explains why hallucinations occur.
icml-2026-detecting-contextual-hallucina.tldr: Rapid local changes in attention provide lightweight features for detecting contextual hallucinations, improving results on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Survival prediction estimates when an event will occur, even when observation ends before the event is seen. That incomplete observation is called censoring. Standard likelihood-based approaches often focus on event prediction and set aside the censoring mechanism. The paper explains that this treatment is justified when censoring is non-informative and shares no parameters with the event-time model.

When event and censoring processes are coupled, ignoring censoring may discard information useful for learning representations. The proposed approach maps observed covariates into latent components associated with the event, censoring, shared confounding information, and irrelevant information. It learns representations for the first three categories and uses that decomposition to improve estimation of the event distribution.

The authors apply the method to four deep-learning survival models and evaluate it on ten datasets, including two semi-synthetic and eight real-world datasets. They report consistent gains over strong baselines and several state-of-the-art methods. The results support explicitly modeling the observation process as a source of learning signal, particularly when it is connected to the event being predicted.
icml-2026-explicitly-modeling-censoring-.tldr: Learning separate event, censoring, and shared representations improves survival prediction in experiments across four models and ten datasets.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can involve nested optimization, as in hyperparameter tuning or meta-learning across clients. Standard formulations often assume each client’s data distribution stays fixed. This paper studies what happens when deployed decisions change client behavior and data collection, so both levels of the optimization operate on distributions that depend on the decisions themselves.

The authors define a federated bilevel performatively stable point using a decoupled-risk perspective and establish sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. They propose two methods for computing it. FBi-RRM converges linearly when a contraction condition holds. FBi-SGD uses federated hypergradient estimation to reduce communication and has convergence guarantees with diminishing step sizes when distribution sensitivities are sufficiently small.

Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification support the predicted stability thresholds and show improved meta-generalization over baselines that ignore performativity. Classification with convolutional networks also demonstrates practical effectiveness in nonconvex settings. The contribution links decision-induced distribution changes to both algorithm design and stability conditions, while keeping the formal guarantees tied to the assumptions under which they were established.
icml-2026-federated-bilevel-performative.tldr: The paper develops federated bilevel learning methods for decision-dependent data distributions, with conditional stability guarantees and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Multi-modal object re-identification matches the same object across different kinds of sensor observations. The paper argues that existing methods emphasize low-frequency information, including broad appearance, color, and illumination. This can leave geometric and textural details underused, even though those finer structures help distinguish identities and support alignment across different modalities.

FUSE separates learned features into low-, middle-, and high-frequency subspaces using an adaptive spectral decomposition module. A second module aligns spectral energy across modalities while encouraging the subspaces to provide complementary information. Frequency-consistency regularization supports this alignment, and learnable frequency modulation is included to improve robustness to lighting variation and differences between sensors.

Experiments on RGBNT201, RGBNT100, and MSVR310 report improvements of 9.1% in mean average precision and 9.5% in Rank-1 performance. These findings support representing identity through multiple frequency ranges instead of relying heavily on coarse appearance. The separation also gives the framework an interpretable organization: different parts of the representation correspond to different scales of visual structure, which are then aligned across modalities.
icml-2026-fuse-frequency-domain-unificat.tldr: FUSE separates and aligns visual information across frequency ranges to improve multi-modal object re-identification.

paragraphs: Learning-based methods for difficult combinatorial optimization problems can adapt to patterns in their inputs, but their training may be expensive or unstable and their guarantees limited. Classical approximation algorithms offer worst-case guarantees, yet are non-differentiable and cannot adapt to natural input distributions. This paper investigates how to combine these strengths for Uniform Facility Location.

The proposed model is a fully differentiable message-passing neural network that incorporates principles from approximation algorithms. It does not require solver-provided supervision or discrete relaxations. Its design therefore connects a trainable graph model with algorithmic structure, rather than relying solely on learning to discover an effective solution procedure. The authors establish approximation guarantees for the resulting model.

Empirically, the model improves on standard approximation algorithms and moves closer to the results obtained through integer linear programming. Uniform Facility Location has applications in clustering, summarization, logistics, and supply chains, making the tradeoff practically relevant. The stated result is a method that combines learned adaptation with provable approximation properties; the empirical improvement does not imply that it always finds an exact optimum.
icml-2026-learning-to-approximate-unifor.tldr: A differentiable graph neural network combines approximation guarantees with empirical improvements for Uniform Facility Location.

paragraphs: Traffic forecasting depends on relationships between locations and on how traffic evolves over time. This paper builds a transformer-like network from an explicit optimization procedure. It represents spatial correlations with an undirected graph and temporal sequences with a directed graph, giving the model separate structures for these two kinds of dependence.

The prediction method assumes that the traffic signal is smooth with respect to both graphs. New terms based on the l2 and l1 norms quantify and encourage smoothness on the directed graph. The authors develop an iterative ADMM algorithm, then turn its steps into a feed-forward network whose parameters can be learned from data. Periodic graph-learning modules serve the role of self-attention.

Experiments show forecasting performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods while substantially reducing parameter counts. The architecture is interpretable because its operations originate in a stated optimization problem and graph assumptions. Its efficiency result suggests that this structure can provide a useful alternative to conventional attention mechanisms for traffic prediction, with the smoothness assumption remaining central to how the forecasting problem is formulated.
icml-2026-lightweight-and-interpretable-.tldr: Unrolling a spatial-temporal graph optimization algorithm yields an interpretable traffic forecaster with competitive accuracy and far fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation follows a sequence of reverse transitions toward a data sample. This paper develops a training approach by establishing an equivalence between the likelihood of the target data distribution and a likelihood evaluated along that reverse path. The connection provides a basis for learning the generation process through its successive transitions.

To make this calculation manageable, Likelihood Matching approximates each reverse transition with a Gaussian whose conditional mean and covariance are matched. Maximizing this quasi-likelihood estimates both score and Hessian functions, capturing information used to match the first two transition moments. A stochastic sampler then uses both estimates during generation, connecting the training objective to the sampling procedure.

The authors establish consistency of the quasi-maximum likelihood estimator and finite-sample-style, non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for the sampler. Their error analysis accounts for score and Hessian estimation, dimensionality, and the number of diffusion steps. Empirical and simulation results support the approach and its theory. The contribution is a unified likelihood-based treatment of training and sampling that explicitly tracks errors introduced by estimation and approximation.
icml-2026-likelihood-matching-for-diffus.tldr: Likelihood Matching trains diffusion models through Gaussian approximations of reverse transitions and provides estimation and sampling guarantees.

paragraphs: Semidefinite programs support convex optimization and strong relaxations of difficult combinatorial problems, but large instances can be expensive to solve. Graph neural networks are appealing computational substitutes because they can represent sparse relationships between variables and constraints. This paper asks what architectural expressiveness is sufficient to recover optimal solutions to linear semidefinite programs.

The authors first prove that standard graph neural network architectures cannot recover solutions in general. They then identify a more expressive architecture that captures relevant SDP structure and can emulate the updates of a standard first-order solver. This establishes a concrete link between what the network can represent and the operations needed by an optimization algorithm.

On synthetic instances and several classes from SDPLIB, the more expressive model consistently reduces prediction error and objective gap compared with theoretically weaker baselines. Its predictions also provide effective starting points for a first-order solver, yielding reported speedups of up to 80%. The results connect representational theory to a practical workflow in which learned predictions accelerate an established solver.
icml-2026-on-the-expressive-power-of-gnn.tldr: A more expressive graph architecture overcomes identified limitations of standard GNNs for SDPs and accelerates a solver through better starting points.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a specific mathematical account of rational behavior for reinforcement-learning agents. It defines a perfectly rational deployment action through the steepest direction of improvement in a hidden true value function. Expected rational risk accumulates the value discrepancy between an agent’s actions and their rational counterparts over the trajectory.

The authors also define an empirical training version of this risk. The difference between training and deployment risk is separated into an external component caused by environment changes and an internal component reflecting the algorithm’s generalization. They bound the external component using Wasserstein distances between transition rules and initial-state distributions, and the internal component using the empirical Rademacher complexity of the value-function class.

These bounds motivate hypotheses about regularization, domain randomization, and distribution shift. In particular, the theory suggests benefits from layer normalization, l2 regularization, weight normalization, and domain randomization, alongside harm from environment changes. Experiments agree with those hypotheses. The contribution supplies measures and explanatory theory for this defined notion of rationality, linking deployment behavior to both learning complexity and environmental differences.
icml-2026-rationality-measurement-and-th.tldr: The paper defines rational risk for reinforcement-learning agents and bounds its training-to-deployment gap through environment shift and model complexity.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning needs to improve a language model without allowing destabilizing changes. PPO commonly controls updates by clipping probability ratios for sampled tokens. The paper argues that this is a noisy way to assess changes in a distribution over a large vocabulary, producing uneven constraints across tokens with different probabilities.

According to the authors’ analysis, clipping can penalize updates to unlikely tokens too strongly while insufficiently limiting large changes to likely tokens. Their alternative, Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization, constrains updates using a direct estimate of distributional divergence, such as Total Variation or KL. Binary and Top-K approximations are introduced to capture essential divergence information without the memory cost of a full calculation.

Empirical evaluations report better stability and efficiency than existing methods, with negligible overhead from the proposed approximations. The significance is the connection between how update size is measured and how reliably training proceeds. DPPO replaces a token-level proxy with an estimate aimed more directly at the policy distribution, and the reported experiments support that choice for language-model fine-tuning.
icml-2026-rethinking-the-trust-region-in.tldr: DPPO replaces PPO’s sampled-token clipping with efficient divergence estimates, improving reported stability and efficiency in language-model reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Data-free quantization uses synthesized examples to prepare lower-precision models without accessing real data. For vision Transformers, those examples may differ from the input distribution that the quantized model needs, reducing performance. MaskAQ addresses this mismatch by focusing synthesis and alignment on the image regions that carry useful semantic information.

The paper identifies a sparse subset of patches, called informative regions, that dominates the mutual information between synthetic inputs and quantized outputs. An entropy-based objective over patch similarity helps separate these regions from noisy backgrounds. A masked attention objective then selects informative regions for aligning the full-precision and quantized models, tailoring synthetic samples to the particular quantized model.

Because that model changes during training, MaskAQ periodically refreshes the synthetic samples to preserve their usefulness. Experiments across multiple backbones and downstream tasks support improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The approach links sample quality to both spatial selectivity and continued adaptation: it concentrates alignment on informative patches while updating the training material as the quantized model evolves.
icml-2026-selective-coupling-of-decouple.tldr: MaskAQ improves data-free vision Transformer quantization by aligning informative image patches and periodically refreshing synthetic training samples.

paragraphs: Language-model deployment faces memory and bandwidth demands from weights and the key-value cache. Low-rank compression offers a hardware-friendly way to reduce these costs, but existing methods can trade reconstruction quality against the time needed to compress a model. Swift-SVD aims to combine optimal layer-wise approximation with practical efficiency and numerical stability.

The framework accumulates the covariance of output activations across input batches and performs one eigenvalue decomposition after aggregation. This produces an activation-aware, closed-form approximation without training. It also uses effective rank to assess how compressible individual layers are. A dynamic allocation strategy assigns ranks while considering both local reconstruction loss and each layer’s importance to the complete model.

Across six language models and eight datasets, Swift-SVD outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and reduces end-to-end compression time by factors of 3–70. Those speedups concern the compression procedure itself. The theoretical optimality applies to the stated layer-wise low-rank approximation problem, while the experiments demonstrate the practical value of combining that solution with a rank allocation strategy informed by whole-model importance.
icml-2026-swift-svd-theoretical-optimali.tldr: Swift-SVD provides training-free, optimal layer-wise low-rank approximation and reports 3–70× faster end-to-end compression.

paragraphs: Predictive coding networks infer internal states through repeated energy minimization using operations that are local in space and time. They work well in shallow architectures, but performance deteriorates beyond roughly five to seven layers. This paper investigates why increasing depth disrupts their training and proposes targeted changes for the identified causes.

The authors find exponentially imbalanced errors across layers and predictions from earlier layers that inadequately guide deeper weight updates. They address these problems with precision-weighted latent-variable optimization during relaxation and a revised weight-update mechanism that reduces error accumulation. For architectures with skip connections, they identify a further timing mismatch: energy travels through residual paths faster than through the main pathway.

Auxiliary neurons slow energy propagation through those residual connections, addressing that third issue. In experiments, the combined methods achieve performance comparable to backpropagation on deep architectures including ResNets. The findings indicate that depth-related failures can be addressed through the balance and propagation of learning signals, providing empirical support for extending predictive coding to more complex models rather than restricting it to shallow networks.
icml-2026-towards-the-training-of-deeper.tldr: Balancing errors, revising weight updates, and slowing residual energy propagation enables deep predictive coding models to perform comparably to backpropagation.

paragraphs: Gene regulatory network inference seeks relationships that help explain how genes regulate cellular activity. Single-cell foundation models offer rich representations of transcriptomic data, but the paper finds their regulatory predictions disappointing. The authors attribute this mainly to reconstruction-based pre-training objectives that do not explicitly encourage the models to capture hidden regulatory signals.

The paper introduces a benchmark focused on generalization to unseen genes and datasets. This tests the zero-shot capabilities of single-cell foundation models and poses a particular challenge for traditional methods. It also proposes Virtual Value Perturbation and Gradient Trajectory, two techniques for extracting implicit regulatory information and converting it into features that describe relationships between genes.

Extensive experiments show that the resulting approach significantly outperforms existing methods. The contribution joins an evaluation target with a way to extract information suited to that target: regulatory features should remain useful beyond the genes and datasets already encountered. The findings support the presence of useful implicit regulatory knowledge in foundation models, while showing that ordinary transcriptomic encoding alone does not reliably expose it.
icml-2026-towards-universal-gene-regulat.tldr: Two extraction methods turn implicit knowledge in single-cell foundation models into regulatory features that generalize to unseen genes and datasets.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a small model propose tokens that a larger target model checks in parallel. Speed depends on how many proposals the target accepts. A limited draft model may approximate the target poorly, shortening accepted sequences. OnlineSPEC uses the verification feedback already produced by this process to improve the draft continuously.

The paper frames repeated drafting, feedback, and adaptation as an online learning problem. Through dynamic regret minimization, it establishes a formal connection between online learning performance and system acceleration. One proposed approach reuses historical gradients as predictive hints for updates. Another maintains multiple draft models through online ensemble learning, allowing the framework to adapt its use of drafts over time.

The algorithms come with theoretical justifications and improved acceleration rates, and experiments across seven benchmarks and five foundation models report speedups of up to 24%. The central opportunity is that verification already reveals discrepancies between draft and target predictions. Reusing that feedback turns an existing checking operation into a learning signal for improving subsequent speculative generation.
icml-2026-when-drafts-evolve-speculative.tldr: OnlineSPEC adapts speculative draft models using existing verification feedback, linking online learning to acceleration and reporting speedups up to 24%.

paragraphs: Language models are often asked to compare generated responses and decide which is better. Combining several judges can help, but simple averaging treats their judgments as equally reliable. This paper shows that comparison probabilities can be inconsistent and that such inconsistencies limit direct probability-based ranking, particularly when no human labels are available for calibration.

The proposed BT-σ model extends Bradley-Terry ranking with a separate discriminator parameter for each judge. It jointly estimates item rankings and judge reliability from pairwise comparisons alone. This allows the aggregation procedure to account for differences between judges instead of assigning every model the same influence by assumption.

On natural-language-generation evaluation benchmarks, BT-σ consistently outperforms averaging-based aggregation. Its learned discriminator parameters strongly correlate with independent measures of cycle consistency, which assess coherence among linked comparisons. Further analysis interprets the method as unsupervised calibration. The findings support estimating reliability within the aggregation process itself, providing a way to improve collective assessment when external human supervision for judge calibration is unavailable.
icml-2026-who-can-we-trust-llm-as-a-jury.tldr: BT-σ jointly learns response rankings and LLM-judge reliability from pairwise comparisons, improving aggregation without human calibration labels.
